name: Babesia spp.

taxonomy.rank_note: Reference groups can include multiple species. Protozoan higher-rank systems differ; the lineage is provided without forcing every clade into a class rank.

morphology: Small intraerythrocytic rings and paired pear-shaped forms; occasional tetrads form a Maltese-cross pattern.
No malarial pigment is produced; forms may be pleomorphic or appear extracellularly. Size varies by species and stage.

transmission.detail: Ticks transmit parasites that multiply in erythrocytes; transfusion can also transmit infection without tick exposure.

life_cycle.detail: Ticks transmit parasites that multiply in erythrocytes; transfusion can also transmit infection without tick exposure.

hosts: Vertebrate hosts include many mammals; humans are incidental hosts for several species. Ticks are vectors and support sexual stages.
distribution: Human cases are best documented in temperate regions; in Thai practice consider travel, tick and transfusion history rather than assuming common endemic infection.
clinical_significance: Fever and hemolytic anemia; severe disease particularly affects asplenic or immunocompromised people.
diagnostics: Giemsa thin films near 1000× with molecular confirmation; interpret parasitemia through validated laboratory procedures.
differential_diagnosis: Early malaria rings can look similar; tetrads support Babesia but may be absent. Morphology alone may not resolve species.
review_status: Source-compiled educational content; not independently clinically validated

annotation_guidance: Record specimen, stage, stain, objective/total magnification, pixel calibration, source image and reviewer certainty.
Native crops of 200–650 pixels do not determine biological size. Retain µm-per-pixel calibration before resizing.
Split training, validation and test data by patient/specimen; keep related crops in the same split.
Keep damaged or ambiguous objects uncertain. Molecular confirmation of a mixed specimen does not assign every pictured object a species.
Separate thick and thin films; retain erythrocyte context for malaria and full head/tail context for microfilariae.
